title: HealBench: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Evaluating Psychological Comfort in Text-to-Image Generation

paper.title: HealBench: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Evaluating Psychological Comfort in Text-to-Image Generation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Current text-to-image and image-editing models can generate photorealistic images with strong semantic fidelity and high visual quality. Yet an important human-centered capability remains underexplored: whether these systems can create images that users perceive as psychologically comforting. Drawing on cognitive evaluation theory, we conceptualize psychological comfort not as a low-level visual property, but as an affective response shaped by a viewer’s appraisal of restorative and emotionally supportive cues.
To study this problem, we introduce HealBench, a large-scale, fine-grained benchmark for evaluating perceived psychological comfort in restorative visual stimuli. HealBench contains 30K high-quality image-text pairs spanning 19 high-level categories and 92 subcategories, constructed from 100K candidates through a human-and-expert-in-the-loop pipeline. To preserve the restorative nature of the data, the pipeline integrates VLM-based semantic matching, multiple human preference models, expert filtering, and augmentation guided by highly restorative exemplars. We further construct HealBench-Eval, a rigorously selected evaluation set of 1,095 instances using feature clustering.
Using HealBench-Eval, we conduct extensive objective and subjective evaluations of 14 representative image generation models, together with prompt-rewriting generation strategies. Our results reveal a clear gap between conventional visual generation quality and perceived psychological comfort: models that perform well on semantic alignment and aesthetics still struggle to produce images experienced as emotionally restorative. Further reinforcement learning experiments show that HealScorer can serve as a practical reward signal for assessing and improving the emotional and restorative quality of generated images. These findings suggest that psychological comfort is a distinct and underexplored dimension of human-centered image generation, and establish HealBench as a foundation for future work on affect-aware generative models.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Recently, text-to-image (T2I) generation and instruction-guided image editing have made rapid progress in semantic alignment ( Fu et al. 2025b ) , visual quality, editing fidelity ( Yu et al. 2025 ; Fu et al. 2025a ) , and human preference modeling ( Ma et al. 2025 ) . These advances have enabled generative models to produce images that are increasingly faithful, realistic, and visually appealing. However, as visual generation systems are increasingly used in emotionally sensitive and human-centered scenarios, a more subtle question emerges: can a generated image not only look correct , but also feel right to the viewer? This distinction matters when images are expected to support emotional experience, restoration, or psychological relief rather than merely satisfy semantic or aesthetic criteria. An image may match the prompt and appear visually polished, yet still fail to provide perceived psychological comfort ( Belanche et al. 2025 ) . HealBench organizes healing-related visual content into 19 categories and 92 subcategories, which are further grouped into six major classes according to different healing functions. For each category, we present both real-world examples and enhanced images generated via SD 3.5-L, which is also used for dataset augmentation. We argue that this limitation is not merely a weakness of current models, but also a consequence of how the target has been formulated and evaluated. Existing generation pipelines are typically optimized for text-image alignment, perceptual quality, editing fidelity, or generic human preference. These objectives are valuable, but they do not directly capture the affective and restorative experience required by psychological comfort. In particular, current systems suffer from three mismatches. First, there is a target mismatch : perceived psychological comfort depends on affective and restorative cues that are not explicitly captured by existing optimization targets ( Shi et al. 2025 ; Belanche et al. 2025 ; Ortega et al. 2025 ) . Second, there is an evaluation-granularity mismatch : comfort-related failure may arise from different sources, including prompt misalignment, incorrect healing semantics, or poor image quality ( Gao et al. 2025 ; Ortega et al. 2025 ) . As illustrated in Figure 1 , two images may receive similarly low comfort ratings for fundamentally different reasons, making a single scalar score insufficient for diagnostic evaluation. Third, there is a benchmark-and-feedback mismatch : as summarized in Table 1 , existing benchmarks and evaluators mainly target preference, alignment, fidelity, compositionality, or generic quality, but do not explicitly target perceived psychological comfort or provide actionable, rationale-bearing feedback. Against this background, we ask: how can perceived psychological comfort be turned into an evaluable and optimization-relevant objective for image generation and image editing? Rather than treating comfort as a vague holistic preference, we formulate healing-oriented generation through three necessary dimensions: text-image alignment , heal accuracy , and image quality . A generated image should be considered healing only when it satisfies all three dimensions; failure in any one dimension is sufficient to disqualify the output. Accordingly, our goal is not merely to rank images from better to worse, but to identify whether, where, and why a generated image fails to provide perceived psychological comfort. Based on this formulation, we propose HealBench (shown in Figure 2 ), a fine-grained benchmark for evaluating the perceived psychological comfort of generated images. HealBench is constructed through a human-and-expert-in-the-loop pipeline that curates high-quality data from a large-scale candidate image-text pool, performs imitative data augmentation, and builds a rigorously filtered test set for unified comparison across models and prompting strategies. Unlike preference-style benchmarks that primarily produce aggregate scores, HealBench is designed around failure-based diagnosis: it identifies whether an output violates text-image alignment, heal accuracy, or image quality, thereby revealing different ways in which a generated image may fail to be healing. Evaluation alone, however, is insufficient for improving generation systems. To make diagnosis actionable, we introduce a score-plus-rationale feedback paradigm, where each result is paired with both a comfort score and an explicit explanation of which dimension fails and why. This structured feedback supports prompt rewriting for both T2I generation and instruction-guided image editing. Since large-scale model iteration cannot rely entirely on costly human evaluation, we further train an automatic evaluator, Tri-dimensional Healing Scorer ( THS ), on top of HealBench to approximate these structured judgments and study its use as an optimization signal for downstream improvement, including RL-based fine-tuning. Within this work, we treat psychological comfort as a distinct human-centered objective for visual generation, rather than as a by-product of semantic alignment, aesthetics, or generic preference. Our contributions are as follows: (1)We formulate perceived psychological comfort as a failure-based evaluation problem for healing-oriented visual generation, defined by three necessary dimensions: text-image alignment , heal accuracy , and image quality . (2)We build HealBench , a fine-grained benchmark that diagnoses whether a generated image fails on any of the three dimensions, instead of relying solely on aggregate preference-style scoring. (3)We introduce a score-plus-rationale feedback paradigm and THS , turning structured diagnosis into an actionable signal for prompt refinement and downstream model optimization.

sections.heading: Related Work
sections.text: Image Generation and Editing Models. Recent visual generation models have made substantial progress in fidelity, semantic alignment, controllability, and human preference alignment. Diffusion models such as DDPM, latent diffusion, Imagen, and DiT enable high-resolution synthesis and strong prompt following ( Ho et al. 2020 ; Rombach et al. 2022 ; Saharia et al. 2022 ; Peebles and Xie 2023 ) ; autoregressive and token-based models such as DALL ⋅ \cdot E, Make-A-Scene, and Muse improve complex content modeling and composition ( Ramesh et al. 2021 ; Gafni et al. 2022 ; Chang et al. 2023 ) ; and flow-matching or rectified-flow methods further enhance training and sampling efficiency ( Lipman et al. 2023 ; Liu et al. 2025 ; Esser et al. 2024 ) . Preference optimization and reinforcement learning methods further align T2I models with human judgments ( Black et al. 2024 ; Fan et al. 2023 ; Wallace et al. 2024 ) , while text-guided editing methods provide instruction-based control over image content and style ( Hertz et al. 2023 ; Mokady et al. 2023 ; Brooks et al. 2023 ) . However, these methods mainly optimize whether images are faithful, realistic, editable, or generally preferred. Existing affective methods, such as Affective Image Filter and EmoEdit, focus on explicit emotion cues or targeted emotional editing ( Weng et al. 2023 ; Yang et al. 2025 ) , leaving subtler outcomes such as psychological comfort, safety, companionship, and healing underexplored. Text-to-Image Evaluation Benchmarks and Metrics. Existing T2I evaluation primarily targets semantic correctness, visual quality, compositional reasoning, and generic preference. CLIP-based metrics estimate text-image alignment ( Radford et al. 2021 ) ; reward and preference models such as PickScore, ImageReward, HPS, and HPSv3 capture overall human preference ( Kirstain et al. 2023 ; Xu et al. 2023 ; Wu et al. 2023 ; Ma et al. 2025 ) ; and aesthetic metrics such as AVA and NIMA assess visual appeal ( Murray et al. 2012 ; Talebi and Milanfar 2018 ) . Broader benchmarks, including DrawBench, GenEval, T2I-CompBench, VQAScore / GenAI-Bench, and HEIM, evaluate compositionality, spatial relations, reasoning, robustness, safety, and overall quality ( Saharia et al. 2022 ; Ghosh et al. 2023 ; Huang et al. 2023 ; Lee et al. 2023 ; Lin et al. 2024 ; Li et al. 2024 ) . Yet these metrics mainly ask whether an image is correct, high-quality, or preferred, rather than whether it is psychologically comforting. Although HRS-Bench introduces emotion-grounded evaluation ( Bakr et al. 2023 ) , and HEIM and GenAI-Bench cover broad evaluation dimensions ( Lee et al. 2023 ; Li et al. 2024 ) , deeper affective outcomes such as soothingness and emotional comfort remain insufficiently evaluated. Recent studies further show that metric rankings can be unstable across prompts and protocols ( Wiles et al. 2025 ) , and that faithfulness metrics remain unreliable on challenging subsets ( Saxon et al. 2024 ) . HealBench addresses this gap by treating perceived psychological comfort as a dedicated, fine-grained, and failure-diagnostic evaluation target. Figure 3: Overview of the HealBench construction pipeline. The benchmark is built through three stages: data collection, reward-model-based filtering and augmentation, and tri-dimensional evaluation-criteria generation. Human and expert review is incorporated throughout the pipeline to ensure the quality of both data instances and evaluation criteria. Figure 4: Overview of the two-stage HealScore pipeline. HealScore first evaluates each image with three category-level questions on text-image alignment , heal accuracy , and image quality , and then refines the judgment with six subcategory-level questions. The final score is computed by weighted aggregation of the resulting multi-dimensional responses.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: HealBench is constructed in four stages: (1) taxonomy design and web-video-based image collection; (2) captioning, hierarchical labeling, and reward-model-based filtering; (3) category-aware evaluation protocol construction and HealScore annotation; (4) tri-dimensional scorer training and data augmentation. Experts participate in taxonomy design, question revision, and iterative quality checks, while VLMs/LLMs are used as scalable assistants.

sections.heading: Evaluation Criteria and HealScore
sections.text: Existing image-generation metrics mainly emphasize semantic alignment and aesthetic preference, but are insufficient for evaluating psychological soothing effects. We therefore propose HealScore , a structured metric defined on three dimensions: text-image alignment, heal accuracy, and image quality. Here, heal accuracy refers to the perceived healing degree of the image under its target category, not to clinical efficacy. For each category pair c = ( T i , S i , j ) c=(T_{i},S_{i,j}) , we build a category-aware question set. An LLM first generates one coarse-level question for the general healing function of T i T_{i} and two fine-grained questions for the concrete visual or affective cues of S i , j S_{i,j} under each dimension. Experts then revise the questions to remove ambiguous, redundant, or category-mismatched formulations. The resulting question set is 𝒬 c = { q d , k c ∣ d ∈ { sem , heal , qual } , k ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2 } } , \mathcal{Q}_{c}=\left\{q^{c}_{d,k}\mid d\in\{\text{sem},\text{heal},\text{qual}\},\;k\in\{0,1,2\}\right\}, (3) where q d , 0 c q^{c}_{d,0} is the coarse-level question and q d , 1 c , q d , 2 c q^{c}_{d,1},q^{c}_{d,2} are fine-grained supplementary questions. For each image I ∈ 𝒟 filter I\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{filter}} , an LLM scores every question in 𝒬 c ⁡ ( I ) \mathcal{Q}_{c(I)} on a 1–10 scale. Let the resulting scores be r sem , k ​ ( I ) r_{\text{sem},k}(I) , r heal , k ​ ( I ) r_{\text{heal},k}(I) , and r qual , k ​ ( I ) r_{\text{qual},k}(I) . (4) We report the three dimension scores for diagnosis and use a compact summary score only for ranking, training, and large-scale comparison. Since psychological comfort is the primary objective of the benchmark, the summary score gives the healing dimension twice the weight of the alignment and quality dimensions: HealScore ​ ( I ) = s sem ​ ( I ) + 2 ​ s heal ​ ( I ) + s qual ​ ( I ) . \text{HealScore}(I)=s_{\text{sem}}(I)+2\,s_{\text{heal}}(I)+s_{\text{qual}}(I). To reduce annotation noise, we manually inspect sampled scored results and iteratively refine the question set by expert feedback. The detailed scoring process of HealScore is shown in Fig. 4 . To further enrich the dataset, we select, for each category pair, the top-10 images ranked by HealScore and the top-10 images ranked by the normalized reward-model total score. sections.heading: Benchmarking Baseline T2I Models
sections.text: We next benchmark representative diffusion and flow-matching T2I models under the original prompts on healing-oriented generation. Table 3 reports standard metrics as reference baselines. Recent models perform strongly on Aesthetic score, CLIPScore, PickScore, and HPSv3, sometimes exceeding the real-image reference on individual metrics. Because these metrics do not target perceived psychological comfort, they should not be treated as evidence of healing-oriented generation quality. Overall healing-oriented performance. Table 4 shows clear gaps across model families. Among original baselines, Playground v2.5 (25.088), PixArt-XL (25.080), and Hunyuan-DiT (25.020) perform best overall, while SDXL Turbo (18.765) and SD 2.1 (19.390) lag behind. Even when advanced generators approach the real-image reference, their scores remain uneven across dimensions and healing functions. Tri-dimensional analysis. In Table 4 , the three dimensions reveal why aggregate scores are insufficient. Strong baselines usually score above 6.0 on Text-Image Alignment and Image Quality , but are lower and more variable on Heal Accuracy : Playground v2.5 obtains 6.479/6.422 on Alignment/Quality but 6.094 on Heal Accuracy, and SD 3.5 Medium obtains 6.321/6.075 but 5.884. Thus, perceived healing degree cannot be inferred from alignment or visual quality alone. Class-level analysis. As shown in Table 4 , Class-wise results further show uneven difficulty. Living Companionship is often easiest, reaching 29.624 for Sana-1.6B , 29.759 for FLUX.1 [dev] , and 29.057 for SD 3.5 Large . In contrast, Shelter and Safety and Natural Restoration show larger model-dependent variation, and no model dominates all six classes. HealBench therefore exposes both dimension-specific and function-specific limitations. Figure 6: Qualitative examples of our prompt rewriting strategy. Using the same image generation model, targeted prompt rewriting markedly improves generation outcomes, yielding more coherent and safer images with substantially higher HealScores across multiple categories.

For editing, rewritten prompts improve both Pix2Pix and SDXL-Pix2Pix in overall HealScore and all three dimensions. Qualitative analysis. sections.heading: THS as an Automatic Healing Scorer
sections.text: We next examine whether THS can provide a more suitable automatic evaluation signal for healing-oriented generation than generic scoring models. To this end, we compare THS with several widely used baselines, including PickScore, LAION Aesthetic, CLIPScore, and HPSv3, using the same pairwise ranking protocol as in the preference validation experiment. As shown in Table 6 , THS substantially outperforms all generic baselines across all three ranking metrics, achieving 0.8527 in Accuracy, 0.7741 in Kendall’s τ \tau , and 0.9223 in Spearman’s ρ \rho . By contrast, the generic scorers remain far behind, with Accuracy values clustered around 0.50–0.56 and much weaker rank correlation. These results indicate that existing scoring models for semantics, aesthetics, or broad human preference do not adequately capture the specific notion of perceived psychological comfort targeted in this work. Results justify the need for a task-specific automatic scorer. Rather than serving only as a descriptive metric, THS provides a scalable evaluation signal that is better aligned with healing-oriented preference and can therefore support both large-scale benchmarking and downstream optimization. sections.heading: Exploratory RL Fine-Tuning with THS Reward
sections.text: Finally, we conduct a preliminary study to examine whether THS can serve not only as an evaluator, but also as a reward signal for direct model optimization. To this end, we fine-tune SD 3.5 Medium with Flow-GRPO using a reward defined by a weighted combination of THS and CLIPScore. As shown in Table 7 , the Flow-GRPO fine-tuned model improves over the base SD 3.5 Medium across all four metrics, including Overall (23.47 → \rightarrow 25.67), Semantic (6.12 → \rightarrow 6.48), Heal (5.73 → \rightarrow 6.45), and Quality (5.88 → \rightarrow 6.28). Notably, the largest gain appears on the Heal dimension, which is consistent with the role of THS as a healing-oriented reward signal. This suggests that the proposed scorer is not only useful for benchmark evaluation, but can also provide an effective optimization signal for improving healing-oriented generation. We emphasize that this experiment is exploratory rather than a fully optimized RL recipe. Nevertheless, the consistent gains across all dimensions provide initial evidence that THS can support downstream alignment toward psychologically comforting image generation.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: We present HealBench , the first fine-grained benchmark for evaluating perceived psychological comfort in text-to-image generation and image editing. By explicitly defining healing-oriented generation along three complementary dimensions ( text-image alignment , heal accuracy , and image quality ), we move psychological comfort from an implicit notion of preference to a structured and measurable objective. Building on this formulation, we develop a large-scale human-and-expert-in-the-loop benchmark, introduce the rule-based HealScore , and further propose THS , a learnable automatic evaluator. Our experiments reveal a clear gap between strong performance on conventional generation metrics and true effectiveness under healing-oriented evaluation. Beyond benchmarking, we show that structured score-plus-rationale feedback can directly support generation improvement, and that the HEAL taxonomy provides a useful basis for personalized healing-content delivery. In conclusion, our results establish psychological comfort as a distinct evaluation and optimization target in generative vision, and position HealBench as a strong foundation for future work on affect-aware, human-centered multimodal generation.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.27516v1 [cs.CV] 20 Oct 2026 \tl_set:Ne \bluebadge bluebadge \tl_set:Ne \greenbudge greenbudge HealBench: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Evaluating Psychological Comfort in Text-to-Image Generation Junjie Xu Yuzhe Yang Rui Yang Luwei Xiao Wenxin Hu Xingjiao Wu Liang He Abstract Current text-to-image and image-editing models can generate photorealistic images with strong semantic fidelity and high visual quality. Yet an important human-centered capability remains underexplored: whether these systems can create images that users perceive as psychologically comforting. Drawing on cognitive evaluation theory, we conceptualize psychological comfort not as a low-level visual property, but as an affective response shaped by a viewer’s appraisal of restorative and emotionally supportive cues. To study this problem, we introduce HealBench, a large-scale, fine-grained benchmark for evaluating perceived psychological comfort in restorative visual stimuli. HealBench contains 30K high-quality image-text pairs spanning 19 high-level categories and 92 subcategories, constructed from 100K candidates through a human-and-expert-in-the-loop pipeline. To preserve the restorative nature of the data, the pipeline integrates VLM-based semantic matching, multiple human preference models, expert filtering, and augmentation guided by highly restorative exemplars. We further construct HealBench-Eval, a rigorously selected evaluation set of 1,095 instances using feature clustering. Using HealBench-Eval, we conduct extensive objective and subjective evaluations of 14 representative image generation models, together with prompt-rewriting generation strategies. Our results reveal a clear gap between conventional visual generation quality and perceived psychological comfort: models that perform well on semantic alignment and aesthetics still struggle to produce images experienced as emotionally restorative. Further reinforcement learning experiments show that HealScorer can serve as a practical reward signal for assessing and improving the emotional and restorative quality of generated images. These findings suggest that psychological comfort is a distinct and underexplored dimension of human-centered image generation, and establish HealBench as a foundation for future work on affect-aware generative models. 1 East China Normal University 2 Johns Hopkins University 3 National University of Singapore Keywords: Text-to-Image, Emotional Comfort, Benchmark and datasets, Image Manipulation, Multi-modal Learning Introduction Recently, text-to-image (T2I) generation and instruction-guided image editing have made rapid progress in semantic alignment ( Fu et al. 2025b ) , visual quality, editing fidelity ( Yu et al. 2025 ; Fu et al. 2025a ) , and human preference modeling ( Ma et al. 2025 ) . These advances have enabled generative models to produce images that are increasingly faithful, realistic, and visually appealing. However, as visual generation systems are increasingly used in emotionally sensitive and human-centered scenarios, a more subtle question emerges: can a generated image not only look correct , but also feel right to the viewer? This distinction matters when images are expected to support emotional experience, restoration, or psychological relief rather than merely satisfy semantic or aesthetic criteria. An image may match the prompt and appear visually polished, yet still fail to provide perceived psychological comfort ( Belanche et al. 2025 ) . HealBench organizes healing-related visual content into 19 categories and 92 subcategories, which are further grouped into six major classes according to different healing functions. For each category, we present both real-world examples and enhanced images generated via SD 3.5-L, which is also used for dataset augmentation. We argue that this limitation is not merely a weakness of current models, but also a consequence of how the target has been formulated and evaluated. Existing generation pipelines are typically optimized for text-image alignment, perceptual quality, editing fidelity, or generic human preference. These objectives are valuable, but they do not directly capture the affective and restorative experience required by psychological comfort. In particular, current systems suffer from three mismatches. First, there is a target mismatch : perceived psychological comfort depends on affective and restorative cues that are not explicitly captured by existing optimization targets ( Shi et al. 2025 ; Belanche et al. 2025 ; Ortega et al. 2025 ) . Second, there is an evaluation-granularity mismatch : comfort-related failure may arise from different sources, including prompt misalignment, incorrect healing semantics, or poor image quality ( Gao et al. 2025 ; Ortega et al. 2025 ) . As illustrated in Figure 1 , two images may receive similarly low comfort ratings for fundamentally different reasons, making a single scalar score insufficient for diagnostic evaluation. Third, there is a benchmark-and-feedback mismatch : as summarized in Table 1 , existing benchmarks and evaluators mainly target preference, alignment, fidelity, compositionality, or generic quality, but do not explicitly target perceived psychological comfort or provide actionable, rationale-bearing feedback. Against this background, we ask: how can perceived psychological comfort be turned into an evaluable and optimization-relevant objective for image generation and image editing? Rather than treating comfort as a vague holistic preference, we formulate healing-oriented generation through three necessary dimensions: text-image alignment , heal accuracy , and image quality . A generated image should be considered healing only when it satisfies all three dimensions; failure in any one dimension is sufficient to disqualify the output. Accordingly, our goal is not merely to rank images from better to worse, but to identify whether, where, and why a generated image fails to provide perceived psychological comfort. Based on this formulation, we propose HealBench (shown in Figure 2 ), a fine-grained benchmark for evaluating the perceived psychological comfort of generated images. HealBench is constructed through a human-and-expert-in-the-loop pipeline that curates high-quality data from a large-scale candidate image-text pool, performs imitative data augmentation, and builds a rigorously filtered test set for unified comparison across models and prompting strategies. Unlike preference-style benchmarks that primarily produce aggregate scores, HealBench is designed around failure-based diagnosis: it identifies whether an output violates text-image alignment, heal accuracy, or image quality, thereby revealing different ways in which a generated image may fail to be healing. Evaluation alone, however, is insufficient for improving generation systems. To make diagnosis actionable, we introduce a score-plus-rationale feedback paradigm, where each result is paired with both a comfort score and an explicit explanation of which dimension fails and why. This structured feedback supports prompt rewriting for both T2I generation and instruction-guided image editing. Since large-scale model iteration cannot rely entirely on costly human evaluation, we further train an automatic evaluator, Tri-dimensional Healing Scorer ( THS ), on top of HealBench to approximate these structured judgments and study its use as an optimization signal for downstream improvement, including RL-based fine-tuning. Within this work, we treat psychological comfort as a distinct human-centered objective for visual generation, rather than as a by-product of semantic alignment, aesthetics, or generic preference. Our contributions are as follows: (1)We formulate perceived psychological comfort as a failure-based evaluation problem for healing-oriented visual generation, defined by three necessary dimensions: text-image alignment , heal accuracy , and image quality . (2)We build HealBench , a fine-grained benchmark that diagnoses whether a generated image fails on any of the three dimensions, instead of relying solely on aggregate preference-style scoring. (3)We introduce a score-plus-rationale feedback paradigm and THS , turning structured diagnosis into an actionable signal for prompt refinement and downstream model optimization. Related Work Image Generation and Editing Models. Recent visual generation models have made substantial progress in fidelity, semantic alignment, controllability, and human preference alignment. Diffusion models such as DDPM, latent diffusion, Imagen, and DiT enable high-resolution synthesis and strong prompt following ( Ho et al. 2020 ; Rombach et al. 2022 ; Saharia et al. 2022 ; Peebles and Xie 2023 ) ; autoregressive and token-based models such as DALL ⋅ \cdot E, Make-A-Scene, and Muse improve complex content modeling and composition ( Ramesh et al. 2021 ; Gafni et al. 2022 ; Chang et al. 2023 ) ; and flow-matching or rectified-flow methods further enhance training and sampling efficiency ( Lipman et al. 2023 ; Liu et al. 2025 ; Esser et al. 2024 ) . Preference optimization and reinforcement learning methods further align T2I models with human judgments ( Black et al. 2024 ; Fan et al. 2023 ; Wallace et al. 2024 ) , while text-guided editing methods provide instruction-based control over image content and style ( Hertz et al. 2023 ; Mokady et al. 2023 ; Brooks et al. 2023 ) . However, these methods mainly optimize whether images are faithful, realistic, editable, or generally preferred. Existing affective methods, such as Affective Image Filter and EmoEdit, focus on explicit emotion cues or targeted emotional editing ( Weng et al. 2023 ; Yang et al. 2025 ) , leaving subtler outcomes such as psychological comfort, safety, companionship, and healing underexplored. Text-to-Image Evaluation Benchmarks and Metrics. Existing T2I evaluation primarily targets semantic correctness, visual quality, compositional reasoning, and generic preference. CLIP-based metrics estimate text-image alignment ( Radford et al. 2021 ) ; reward and preference models such as PickScore, ImageReward, HPS, and HPSv3 capture overall human preference ( Kirstain et al. 2023 ; Xu et al. 2023 ; Wu et al. 2023 ; Ma et al. 2025 ) ; and aesthetic metrics such as AVA and NIMA assess visual appeal ( Murray et al. 2012 ; Talebi and Milanfar 2018 ) . Broader benchmarks, including DrawBench, GenEval, T2I-CompBench, VQAScore / GenAI-Bench, and HEIM, evaluate compositionality, spatial relations, reasoning, robustness, safety, and overall quality ( Saharia et al. 2022 ; Ghosh et al. 2023 ; Huang et al. 2023 ; Lee et al. 2023 ; Lin et al. 2024 ; Li et al. 2024 ) . Yet these metrics mainly ask whether an image is correct, high-quality, or preferred, rather than whether it is psychologically comforting. Although HRS-Bench introduces emotion-grounded evaluation ( Bakr et al. 2023 ) , and HEIM and GenAI-Bench cover broad evaluation dimensions ( Lee et al. 2023 ; Li et al. 2024 ) , deeper affective outcomes such as soothingness and emotional comfort remain insufficiently evaluated. Recent studies further show that metric rankings can be unstable across prompts and protocols ( Wiles et al. 2025 ) , and that faithfulness metrics remain unreliable on challenging subsets ( Saxon et al. 2024 ) . HealBench addresses this gap by treating perceived psychological comfort as a dedicated, fine-grained, and failure-diagnostic evaluation target. Figure 3: Overview of the HealBench construction pipeline. The benchmark is built through three stages: data collection, reward-model-based filtering and augmentation, and tri-dimensional evaluation-criteria generation. Human and expert review is incorporated throughout the pipeline to ensure the quality of both data instances and evaluation criteria. Figure 4: Overview of the two-stage HealScore pipeline. HealScore first evaluates each image with three category-level questions on text-image alignment , heal accuracy , and image quality , and then refines the judgment with six subcategory-level questions. The final score is computed by weighted aggregation of the resulting multi-dimensional responses. Method Overview HealBench is constructed in four stages: (1) taxonomy design and web-video-based image collection; (2) captioning, hierarchical labeling, and reward-model-based filtering; (3) category-aware evaluation protocol construction and HealScore annotation; (4) tri-dimensional scorer training and data augmentation. Experts participate in taxonomy design, question revision, and iterative quality checks, while VLMs/LLMs are used as scalable assistants. Data Collection and Filtering We first build a two-level taxonomy for psychologically comforting imagery. Experts define 18 coarse-grained categories, supplemented with an Others class, to cover common restorative visual functions. Conclusion We present HealBench , the first fine-grained benchmark for evaluating perceived psychological comfort in text-to-image generation and image editing. By explicitly defining healing-oriented generation along three complementary dimensions ( text-image alignment , heal accuracy , and image quality ), we move psychological comfort from an implicit notion of preference to a structured and measurable objective. Building on this formulation, we develop a large-scale human-and-expert-in-the-loop benchmark, introduce the rule-based HealScore , and further propose THS , a learnable automatic evaluator. Our experiments reveal a clear gap between strong performance on conventional generation metrics and true effectiveness under healing-oriented evaluation. Beyond benchmarking, we show that structured score-plus-rationale feedback can directly support generation improvement, and that the HEAL taxonomy provides a useful basis for personalized healing-content delivery. In conclusion, our results establish psychological comfort as a distinct evaluation and optimization target in generative vision, and position HealBench as a strong foundation for future work on affect-aware, human-centered multimodal generation.
